added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: has largely been out of the reach for most individuals and wealth managers who aren't going to manage a book of derivatives themselves
added_claims.claim: Portable alpha was an institutional tool for about 40 years and out of reach for individuals and wealth managers who will not run a derivatives book; return stacking packages it as a ticker so the capital-efficient structure can be bought without managing the derivatives.
added_claims.conditions: Needs a fund wrapper that runs the derivatives.

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
added_claims.quote: a risk parity type of bond and equity allocation depending on which level volume run it on um is something like a portable alpha product at the end of the day
added_claims.claim: A levered risk-parity bond and equity allocation (and some QIS products) already works as a portable-alpha product, so investors may hold the concept without knowing it; return stacking makes it explicit.
added_claims.conditions: Depends on the volatility target and leverage used.
added_claims.testable: partly - risk parity exposure decomposes into stacked beta

added_claims.speaker: Adam Butler
added_claims.quote: the ETF wrapper has some tax advantages. It has the intraday liquidity. It has the ease of platform access etc.
added_claims.claim: Wrapper choice is a trade-off: an ETF gives tax efficiency, intraday liquidity and easy platform access, whereas a mutual fund (end-of-day NAV) can trade a wider futures set; the same strategy can run in both.
added_claims.direction: ETF for access, mutual fund for market breadth
added_claims.conditions: US tax treatment; Europe lacks the ETF tax advantage.

added_claims.speaker: Adam Butler
added_claims.quote: The market makers are always going to whenever there's less uh transparency, they're going to widen out and thin out
added_claims.claim: Because market makers cannot see the full basket of an active futures ETF, they widen and thin quotes, so wide spreads are a persistent feature, not a temporary one; the cost is worth it for a one-way buy-and-hold investor.
added_claims.indicator: ETF bid-ask spread and basket transparency
added_claims.conditions: Persistent when underlying markets are less liquid and traded daily.

added_claims.speaker: Adam Butler
added_claims.quote: there's a trade-off between accessibility, liquidity, and the diversity of bets that are available
added_claims.claim: Any fund faces a capacity trade-off: more diverse bets raise expected performance, but liquidity limits what can be traded at size, so at some point the markets you can trade no longer matter to P&L; this holds for hedge funds, mutual funds and ETFs.
added_claims.testable: partly - capacity estimates need liquidity data

added_claims.speaker: Adam Butler
added_claims.quote: you can model a moving average cross by taking by weighting for example uh longer term moving averages positively and shorter term moving averages negatively
added_claims.claim: A grid of time-series momentum lookbacks can span continuous moving-average-crossover trend rules (long averages positive, short negative), so a regression on a lookback grid can mimic them; breakout systems with trailing stops and entry-only vol scaling have far more degrees of freedom and are not spanned.
added_claims.indicator: time-series momentum lookback grid as basis for trend rules
added_claims.conditions: Applies to continuous trend signals, not event-driven breakouts.
added_claims.testable: yes - the span can be tested

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: that comes from what markets are you trading, what trend speeds are you trading, how much risk weight are you giving each market
added_claims.claim: Dispersion among trend managers comes from implementation choices: which markets, which trend speeds, how much risk weight per market and which constraints; a replication fits all these parameters to the index to remove arbitrary dispersion.
added_claims.conditions: Cory's 30-second summary of the bottom-up approach.
added_claims.testable: yes - dispersion attribution to markets, speed and weights

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
added_claims.quote: with the bottom up approach, you don't necessarily have that response function
added_claims.claim: A fixed bottom-up fit cannot adapt if the underlying managers change style (for example shifting to faster trends or different markets), unlike a top-down regression, so recalibration frequency is a design question.
added_claims.conditions: Concern if the index managers' style shifts; Cory answers that annual reruns hardly change the weights.

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: to deliver the beta of the category and we're trying to outperform that over the long run through feed differentials
added_claims.claim: The ETF aims to deliver trend beta and beat the category over the long run through lower fees, while managers who want to add alpha should trade the fat tail of markets (which the mutual fund version does).
added_claims.direction: lower fees give net outperformance of beta
added_claims.conditions: Valid if the replication tracks the beta closely.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare ETF net return with the index net of fees

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: but it's also untethered mechanically from trend following
added_claims.claim: The top-down regression works but is mechanically untethered from trend following, which is why a mechanistic bottom-up system with almost opposite strengths and weaknesses is added; the two have fairly uncorrelated tracking errors.
added_claims.conditions: Top-down has no built-in trend rule.
added_claims.testable: yes - tracking error correlation of the two methods

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: Our replication approach is truly applying trend following signals. I think a lot of people get that wrong when they talk about replication
added_claims.claim: Replication is not divorced from trend following: the 70% bottom-up leg applies true trend signals with parameters fitted to the index, and the 30% top-down leg adds process diversification.
added_claims.conditions: Cory's response to critics of replication.

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: if they're using faster mean reversion models, it could be very difficult to pick that up
added_claims.claim: A top-down regression struggles to capture the fast, multi-day mean-reversion models in the broader CTA index because 20-40 daily observations of 20-40 contracts are not enough to fit them, so it ends up capturing mostly the trend part.
added_claims.indicator: top-down replication of the SG CTA index
added_claims.direction: trend explains most of the CTA index but the mean-reversion part is missed
added_claims.conditions: Gets worse as non-trend sleeves grow.
added_claims.testable: yes - R-squared of CTA index regression on trend only

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: are just going to get squeezed out by lower cost, more efficient data implementations
added_claims.claim: Funds charging performance fees for generic trend will be squeezed out by cheaper implementations of the same beta, while fee room remains for managers with real innovation in fat-tail markets, spreads, breakouts and other differentiators.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to managers whose returns resemble the beta.

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
added_claims.quote: 10 days ago, we had a little bit of a draw down event, I guess, in the CTA space
added_claims.claim: As of 15 April 2025 the CTA space had just had a drawdown (equities and trend both falling), and the host hopes it is early innings and that trend recovers within 30-50 days, a reminder that high-stress payoffs arrive with drawdowns first.

added_claims.speaker: Adam Butler
added_claims.quote: we want to have as much allocated to cash uh funded beta where it makes sense, for example, in equities where it's more cash efficient
added_claims.claim: Stack design: hold equity beta in a cash-funded ETF where that is efficient and top up with S&P futures, while keeping enough cash as collateral for futures strategies, so margin never forces a sale during a drawdown.
added_claims.conditions: Equities are the most cash-efficient to hold funded.
added_claims.testable: yes - margin usage can be audited

added_claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
added_claims.quote: we can do specific short location but we can also get these names on swap
added_claims.claim: A merger-arbitrage ETF avoids the borrow-fee and recall risk on the short hedge leg of stock-for-stock deals by hedging via swaps as an alternative to physical shorts; most deals are cash, so hedging is rarely needed.

corrections.issue: Attributed to Adam Butler. The 15-20 year training-window answer comes from Cory's reply to the recalibration question; Adam only speaks from 'We also, when we were investigating this ...' and then says 'to Corey's point'.
corrections.fix: Cory: fitting trend weights needs 15-20 years of data because a market that produced no P&L in a decade cannot be told apart from one managers did not trade, so rerunning each year will not change weights meaningfully.

corrections.issue: Speaker is given as Adam, but the passage continues without a break from the speaker who gave the coffee example (C09-1, Cory); no change of speaker is shown.
corrections.fix: Same speaker as C09-1 (Cory): large trend managers put about 80% of risk in the same ~20 markets; averaging the fat-tail weights across managers attenuates toward zero, so the beta can be captured with a handful of common markets.

corrections.issue: Attributed to Adam, but the co-host next responds 'to what Corey just said about the blowout risk' and 'I agree with you, Cory', so the passage is Cory's.
corrections.fix: Cory: a high-volatility trend strategy is a capital-efficient version of a low-vol one (50 vol with a fifth of the capital equals 10 vol) and at the limit a portable alpha overlay, ignoring knock-out leverage risk.

corrections.issue: Attributed to Adam, but it is the same passage by Cory (co-host replies 'I agree with you, Cory').
corrections.fix: Cory (citing Cliff Asness): most clients cannot tolerate more than about 10% volatility and line-item risk is too big, so the major players moved to 10-12% vol and products with higher vol struggle.

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - first reader captured every main design point (return stacking, wrapper limits, bottom-up and top-down replication, blend, 18f-4, merger arbitrage, overlays); missed supporting reasons (blend motivation, wrapper trade-offs, dispersion sources, funded beta, fee squeeze) and mislabelled several speakers in the Cory/Adam exchange.
